conflictPolicy.reason: Overwintering habitat takes precedence in late fall. A genus-level 'cut back after flowering' directive (typically given for self-seeding control or tidiness) is deferred to spring rather than applied in late fall, so standing stems remain available to cavity-nesting bees and overwintering pupae. The suppressed directive is not deleted — it stays in the genus rule and still applies in its other seasons — and the leave-stems note carries the spring cut-back instruction.

Hydrangea.note: 51 plants — the largest genus in the catalog. Pruning is the single most consequential call and it splits by species. One plant (Climbing Hydrangea) is a true vine and is handled separately below — it is NOT pruned like the shrub types.

general.note: H. arborescens (smooth hydrangea): once established, prune in spring down to the ground; blooms on new wood. H. paniculata (panicle hydrangea): prune back to a fat bud in fall, late winter, or spring. H. macrophylla (bigleaf hydrangea): buds form in late summer/early fall for next year, so prune right after flowering and before August, or you remove next year's blooms.

source.quote: Astilbes are unforgiving in dry soils, as the leaves will brown quickly

earlySpring.note: Divide vigorously growing clumps every 4-6 years as new foliage emerges.

source.title: Growing Astilbe in Iowa — Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
source.quote: Vigorously growing astilbes can be divided every 4 to 6 years

Syringa.note: 16 plants (lilac). A spring bloomer on old wood — UMN Extension lists lilac among shrubs that must be pruned right after flowering, not in late winter/early spring.

lateSpring.note: Deadhead spent flower clusters and do any shaping right after bloom finishes, before next year's flower buds set — pruning later in the season removes next spring's flowers.

source.title: Pruning Trees and Shrubs — UMN Extension
source.quote: Trees and shrubs that bloom early in the growing season on last year's growth should be pruned immediately after they finish blooming

earlySpring.note: Remove suckers coming up from the roots or low on the trunk; they draw energy without adding to the shrub’s form.

source.title: Pruning trees and shrubs — UMN Extension
source.quote: Remove suckers coming up from the roots or low on the trunk.

Azalea.note: 14 plants. Spring bloomer on old wood, listed by UMN Extension among the shrubs that must be pruned right after flowering rather than in late winter/early spring.

lateSpring.note: Snap or prune off faded flower clusters just after bloom, taking care not to damage the new leaf buds at the base of the flower stalk.

source.title: After the Bloom: Nurturing Your Azaleas and Rhododendrons — NC Cooperative Extension
source.quote: Gently snap or prune off the faded flower trusses just below the flower head, being careful not to damage the developing leaf buds located at the base of the flower stalk.

lateSpring.note: Any shaping or size-control pruning belongs in this same right-after-bloom window — waiting until later removes the buds that would have bloomed next spring.

source.title: Pruning Trees and Shrubs — UMN Extension
source.quote: Trees and shrubs that bloom early in the growing season on last year's growth should be pruned immediately after they finish blooming

Rhododendron.note: 13 plants (large-flowered Rhododendron, kept distinct from Azalea in this catalog). Spring bloomer — pruning window is right after flowering.

lateSpring.note: Snap or prune off faded flower clusters just below the flower head shortly after bloom, taking care not to damage the new leaf buds at the base of the flower stalk — this redirects energy from seed production into next year's buds.

source.title: After the Bloom: Nurturing Your Azaleas and Rhododendrons — NC Cooperative Extension
source.quote: For rhododendrons with larger flower clusters, you might need pruning shears for a clean cut.

lateSpring.note: The window right after flowering is the best time for any shaping or size-control pruning; heavy pruning later risks removing next year's flower buds.

source.title: After the Bloom: Nurturing Your Azaleas and Rhododendrons — NC Cooperative Extension
source.quote: The period immediately after flowering is the ideal time for any necessary pruning.

lateSpring.note: Prune immediately after flowering finishes; because it blooms on old wood, pruning later in the season cuts off next year's flower buds.

source.title: How To Grow and Care for Old Fashioned Weigela — Clemson HGIC
source.quote: Weigela blooms on old wood, so late pruning reduces next year's flowers.

Aster.note: 13 plants (Symphyotrichum spp.) — late-summer/fall bloomers and good Chelsea-chop candidates.

lateSpring.note: Cutting back by about a third to a half in late May/early June (the "Chelsea chop") produces bushier, sturdier plants that are less prone to flopping, with more (if slightly later) bloom.

source.title: Time for the Chelsea Chop! — Mt. Cuba Center
source.quote: The Chelsea chop involves cutting back certain perennials by about one-third to one-half in late May or early June.

earlySpring.note: Divide every 2-3 years to maintain vigor and flower quality.

Iris.note: 13 plants. Mostly rhizomatous iris (bearded, Siberian, Japanese types) — division doubles as pest control.

midSummer.note: Divide every 3-5 years once flowering declines or clumps get crowded; division also helps manage iris borer and soft rot. Best done in July-August, after bloom.

source.title: How to divide and plant bearded iris — Illinois Extension
source.quote: should be divided every three to five years when flowering begins to decline, or the clumps become crowded

midSummer.note: When dividing, discard any rhizome that is soft, mushy, or tunneled by iris borer rather than replanting it.

source.title: How to divide and plant bearded iris — Illinois Extension
source.quote: If you find rhizomes that have iris borer damage, are smelly or mushy (soft rot), discard these rhizomes too.

midSummer.note: Cut foliage back to about a third of its height at division time to reduce water loss and transplant stress.

source.title: How to divide and plant bearded iris — Illinois Extension
source.quote: cut back the leaves to about one-third of their height

Juniperus.note: 15 plants. Evergreen conifer — pruning must stay within live green growth.

general.note: Junipers cannot regenerate from bare, brown wood, so any pruning cut must stay within live green growth — cutting back into a leafless interior leaves a permanent gap.

source.quote: They cannot be severely pruned because they are incapable of initiating new growth from bare branches.
source.title: Pruning Large, Overgrown Shrubs — Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

earlySpring.note: If shaping is needed, prune in late March or early April before new growth begins.

source.quote: Prune evergreen shrubs, such as juniper and yew, in late March or early April before new growth begins.
source.title: Proper Time to Prune Trees and Shrubs — Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

Chamaecyparis.note: 14 plants. Evergreen conifer (false/Hinoki cypress) — same old-wood pruning limits as other conifers.

general.note: Like other evergreen conifers, false cypress will not fill back in if cut into bare, leafless wood — keep any pruning within the green foliage.

source.quote: Do not prune evergreen shrubs back into dead portions of the branches. Any large hole or gap in the canopy revealed by pruning will always remain.
source.title: Pruning Large, Overgrown Shrubs — Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

earlySpring.note: If shaping is needed, prune in late March or early April before new growth begins.

source.quote: Prune evergreen shrubs, such as juniper and yew, in late March or early April before new growth begins.
source.title: Proper Time to Prune Trees and Shrubs — Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

Thuja.note: 11 plants. Arborvitae — very limited ability to regrow from old wood.

general.note: Arborvitae has only limited ability to sprout from bare, old wood, and doing so can take years to fill back in — avoid heavy cuts into the leafless interior.

source.quote: Some species, such as yew and, to a lesser extent, boxwood and arborvitae, can initiate new growth from bare stems and may eventually fill in, but this process can take considerable time.
source.title: Pruning Large, Overgrown Shrubs — Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

earlySpring.note: If shaping is needed, prune in late March or early April before new growth begins.

source.quote: Prune evergreen shrubs, such as juniper and yew, in late March or early April before new growth begins.
source.title: Proper Time to Prune Trees and Shrubs — Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

Cornus.note: 12 plants. Shrub dogwoods (redosier/red-twig group) grown mainly for winter stem color — needs regular renewal pruning to keep that color.

earlySpring.note: Practice renewal pruning: cut the oldest third of stems down to the base every year or two, since the brightest bark color occurs on stems less than 3 years old.

source.title: Redosier dogwood — UMN Extension
source.quote: It is important to practice renewal pruning: remove the oldest third of stems every 1 to 2 years to maintain vibrant color.

Geranium.note: 14 plants. Hardy perennial cranesbill (not tender annual Pelargonium).

earlySummer.note: Shear foliage back lightly after the first bloom flush to revitalize the plant and tidy its shape.

source.title: Geranium sanguineum — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: Foliage may be lightly sheared back and shaped to revitalize after flowering.

Allium.note: 13 plants. Ornamental onion — deadheading is optional, mainly to control self-seeding; foliage should be left to die back on its own.

midSummer.note: Deadheading is optional — it is mainly useful for controlling unwanted self-seeding; otherwise spent flowers/seedheads can be left for winter interest.

source.title: Allium stellatum — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: Deadhead flowers before seed set to help control any unwanted spread.

lateSummer.note: Let foliage die back naturally rather than cutting it early — it persists into or just past flowering before yellowing on its own.

source.title: Allium stellatum — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: Foliage persists to the time of or slightly past flowering in summer before dying back.

Baptisia.note: 13 plants. Deep-taprooted perennial that resents division/transplanting once established; otherwise very low-maintenance.

general.note: Once established, Baptisia develops a deep taproot and expanding clump that should not be divided or transplanted.

source.title: Baptisia australis — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: Over time, plants develop slowly expanding clumps with deep and extensive root systems, and should not be disturbed once established.

earlySummer.note: Optional: trimming/shearing foliage after bloom keeps the plant rounded and can reduce the need for staking, at the cost of the ornamental seed pods.

source.title: Baptisia australis — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: Trimming or shearing foliage after bloom helps maintain rounded plant appearance and obviates a possible need for staking

Achillea.note: 11 plants. Yarrow — deadhead/shear to tidy and rebloom; divide every 2-3 years as it loses vigor and flops.

midSummer.note: Cut back to a lateral flower bud after the initial bloom flush to tidy the planting and encourage additional bloom.

source.title: Achillea millefolium — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: Cutting plants back to lateral flower buds after initial flowering will tidy the planting and encourage additional bloom.

earlySpring.note: Divide clumps every 2-3 years to maintain vigor — plants lose steam and flop in the center if left too long.

source.title: Achillea millefolium — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: Divide clumps as needed (every 2-3 years) to maintain vitality of the planting.

Spiraea.note: 11 plants. Mostly summer-blooming bumald/birchleaf types (bloom on new wood); a couple old-fashioned spring bloomers (Vanhoutte, Grefsheim) bloom on old wood instead and should be pruned right after flowering rather than in spring.

earlySpring.note: Most garden spireas (bumald and birchleaf types, e.g. Anthony Waterer, Goldflame, Goldmound) bloom on the current year's growth and are pruned back in late winter/early spring. A few old-fashioned spring bloomers (Vanhoutte, Grefsheim) bloom on old wood instead and should be pruned right after flowering, not in spring.

source.title: Proper Time to Prune Trees and Shrubs — Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
source.quote: Summer-flowering shrubs, such as potentilla and Japanese spirea, bloom in summer on the current year's growth. Prune summer-flowering shrubs in late winter or early spring.

Anemone.note: 10 plants. Fall-blooming Japanese/hybrid anemones — spreads by rhizomes and can outcompete neighbors if not given room or contained.

general.note: Spreads by rhizomes and forms expanding colonies over time — give it room or be prepared to divide/contain it so it doesn't crowd out neighboring plants.

source.title: Anemone x hybrida 'September Charm' — NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
source.quote: will grow 3 to 4 feet tall and spread 2- to 3 feet wide forming colonies by spreading rhizomes

Ilex.note: 10 plants. Holly — dioecious; female plants need a male of a compatible species/bloom-time nearby to set berries.

general.note: Hollies are dioecious — only one sex per plant. A female plant needs a male holly (same or compatible species, overlapping bloom time) planted nearby to set berries.

source.title: Ilex (Hollies, Holly) — NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
source.quote: Hollies are dioecious, meaning that only one sex is found on any one plant, thus both male and female plants must be grown if fruits are desired.

Rudbeckia.note: 9 plants. Black-eyed Susan — deadhead to extend bloom; self-seeds readily and can spread beyond where it's planted.

midSummer.note: Deadheading can encourage further blooms through the long summer bloom season.

source.title: Rudbeckia (Black-eyed Susan, Coneflower) — NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
source.quote: Deadheading can encourage further blooms

general.note: Typically spreads by self-seeding — deadhead spent flowers before they set seed if volunteer seedlings beyond the planting area aren't wanted.

source.title: Rudbeckia (Black-eyed Susan, Coneflower) — NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
source.quote: typically spread by self-seeding

Liatris.note: 9 plants. Blazing star — dead stems are valuable overwinter, both for stem-nesting native bees and as a food source (goldfinches eat the seeds).

lateFall.note: Native bees nest inside the dead, hollow stems — cut back to 12-24 inches rather than to the ground, and let the cut stems stand until they naturally break down.

source.title: Liatris spicata — NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
source.quote: Native bees nest in the dead, hollow stems, so gardeners are encouraged to cut back dead stems to 12 to 24 inches and allow them to remain standing until they disintegrate on their own.

Helleborus.note: 9 plants. Lenten rose — evergreen foliage goes tattered over winter; the one essential yearly task is cutting back old leaves before flowers open.

earlySpring.note: Old evergreen foliage sprawls and declines over winter — cut it back to the base in late winter, just as the new flower stalks begin to emerge, so blooms aren't hidden behind tattered leaves.

source.title: Lenten Rose — Arkansas Cooperative Extension Service
source.quote: To keep the plant tidy, trim off the old leaves in late winter just as the new crop of shoots begin to emerge.

Pinus.note: 9 plants. Pine (mugo and white pine types) — grows from terminal 'candles' rather than side buds; sizing is controlled by pinching candles, not by cutting into old wood.

lateSpring.note: To control size, pinch or prune off one-half to two-thirds of each new 'candle' in spring while it's still 2-3 inches long and before the needles expand.

source.title: Proper Time to Prune Trees and Shrubs — Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
source.quote: The growth of pines can be slowed by pinching or pruning off one-half to two-thirds of the elongated terminal buds ("candles") in spring when the candles are approximately 2 to 3 inches long.

general.note: Pines don't produce side/lateral buds, so a branch cut back into older growth below the current candles won't resprout — don't rely on hard pruning to reduce size.

source.title: Proper Time to Prune Trees and Shrubs — Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
source.quote: Do not prune branches back to older growth down the stem as new growth will not develop from these areas.

Asclepias.note: 8 plants. Milkweed — the only obligate host plant for monarch caterpillars; avoid pesticides and don't remove plants while caterpillars/eggs may be present.

lateSummer.note: If self-seeding beyond the planting area is a concern, remove immature seed pods before they split open, rather than pulling whole plants.

source.title: Milkweed is taking over my perennial garden — UNH Extension
source.quote: you can prevent further spread by removing immature seed pods

Nepeta.note: 8 plants. Catmint; benefits from a hard shear after first flush to rebloom.

earlySummer.note: Shear back flower spikes after the first flush of bloom to promote continued flowering through summer.

source.title: Nepeta × faassenii — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: Shear flower spikes after initial flowering to promote continued bloom.

Geum.note: 8 plants. Low, clump-forming avens; deadhead for extended bloom and divide to maintain vigor.

midSummer.note: Remove spent flowers to encourage additional bloom, though leaving some later flowers allows attractive fluffy seed heads to form.

source.title: Geum 'Borisii' — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: Remove spent flowers to encourage additional bloom, but consider leaving some of the later flowers so that the fluffy seed heads can form.

earlySpring.note: Divide clumps in spring as needed to maintain plant vigor.

source.title: Geum 'Borisii' — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: Divide plants in spring as needed to maintain vigor.

Veronica.note: 8 plants. Spike speedwell; deadhead spent spikes and cut back after flowering.

midSummer.note: Remove spent flower spikes to encourage additional bloom; plants may be cut back to basal growth after flowering finishes.

source.title: Veronica spicata — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: Remove spent flower spikes to encourage additional bloom. Plants may be cut back to basal growth after flowering.

Amsonia.note: 7 plants. Bluestar; cut back stems after flowering to keep the foliage mound from opening up and flopping.

earlySummer.note: Cut back stems by about 6 inches after flowering to keep stems upright and shape plants into a neat foliage mound.

source.title: Amsonia hubrichtii — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: Consider cutting back the stems by about 6" after flowering to help keep stems upright and to shape plants into a nice foliage mound.

Penstemon.note: 7 plants. Beardtongue; self-sows and can spread beyond its planting spot in garden settings.

general.note: Can spread somewhat aggressively in a garden setting via self-seeding; edit volunteer seedlings if a tighter planting is desired.

source.title: Penstemon digitalis — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: Can spread somewhat aggressively in a garden setting.

Brunnera.note: 7 plants. Siberian bugloss; slowly spreads by rhizome to form a thick ground cover.

general.note: Clumps slowly spread by creeping rhizomes into thick ground covers over time; divide or edge if containment is needed.

source.title: Brunnera macrophylla — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: Clumps slowly spread by creeping rhizomes to form thick ground covers.

Dianthus.note: 7 plants. Cheddar pink; shear the foliage mat after flowering to keep it tidy.

earlySummer.note: After flowering is completed, lightly shear plants back to maximize the ornamental appearance of the foliage mat.

source.title: Dianthus gratianopolitanus — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: After flowering is completed, plants may be lightly sheared back to maximize the ornamental appearance of the foliage mat.

Ligularia.note: 7 plants. Leopard plant; needs consistently moist soil and will wilt in too much sun or dry spells.

general.note: Must have moist soils that never dry out; foliage will wilt if soil dries or plants get too much direct sun.

source.title: Ligularia dentata — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: Must have moist soils that never dry out.

Thymus.note: 7 plants. Creeping thyme; shear to control spread and refresh dense, woody growth.

earlySummer.note: Cut back stems as necessary to maintain plant appearance, control growth and spread, or limit unsightly woody stem growth.

source.title: Thymus serpyllum — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: Cut back stems as necessary to maintain plant appearance, to control growth/spread or to limit unsightly woody stem growth.

Aquilegia.note: 6 plants. Columbine; remove spent flowering stems to prolong bloom and keep soil moist for foliage.

lateSpring.note: Remove flowering stems after bloom to encourage additional bloom; keep soil uniformly moist afterward to prolong the foliage display.

source.title: Aquilegia canadensis — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: Remove flowering stems after bloom to encourage additional bloom.

Solidago.note: 6 plants. Goldenrod; deadhead to tidy and prevent excess self-seeding, and divide every few years to control spread.

lateSummer.note: Remove spent flower clusters to encourage additional bloom and limit self-seeding.

source.title: Solidago rigida — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: Remove spent flower clusters to encourage additional bloom.

earlySpring.note: May need to be divided every 2 to 3 years to control growth and maintain the clump.

source.title: Solidago rigida — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: May need to be divided every 2 to 3 years to control growth.

Aruncus.note: 6 plants. Goat's beard; deadheading is optional and mainly cosmetic since it does not extend bloom.

midSummer.note: Removing faded flower stalks will not prolong bloom, but may improve plant appearance if a tidier look is desired; female plants can also be left in place to enjoy the dried seed plumes.

source.title: Aruncus dioicus — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: Removing faded flower stalks will not prolong bloom, but may improve plant appearance, particularly if a ground cover look is desired.

Lamium.note: 8 plants. Spotted deadnettle; cut back if summer heat causes foliage to melt out.

midSummer.note: If mid-summer foliage decline (melting out) occurs in hot, humid weather, cut plants back or shear them to stimulate fresh new growth.

source.title: Lamium maculatum 'White Nancy' — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: If such mid-summer foliage decline occurs, plants may be cut back or sheared to stimulate new foliage growth.

Diervilla.note: 8 plants. Bush honeysuckle; prune right after flowering since it blooms on old wood.

midSummer.note: Prune as needed immediately after flowering finishes in mid-summer.

source.title: Diervilla lonicera — Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
source.quote: Prune as needed immediately after flowering.

Physocarpus.note: 8 plants. Ninebark; a spring-blooming shrub that tolerates hard renovation pruning but sacrifices that year's flowers.

earlySpring.note: Overgrown plants can be renovated by cutting back hard in late winter/early spring, but as a spring bloomer it will not flower the following spring after such a renovation cut.

source.title: Pruning Large, Overgrown Shrubs — Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
source.quote: Large, overgrown lilacs, honeysuckles, dogwoods, spireas, barberry, flowering quince, ninebark, smokebush, and forsythias may be pruned in this manner. Spring-blooming shrubs like ninebark, smokebush, and forsythia will not bloom the following spring after renovation pruning.

Cotinus.note: 7 plants. Smokebush; a spring-blooming shrub that tolerates hard renovation pruning but sacrifices that year's flowers.

earlySpring.note: Overgrown plants can be renovated by cutting back hard in late winter/early spring, but as a spring bloomer it will not flower the following spring after such a renovation cut.

source.title: Pruning Large, Overgrown Shrubs — Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
source.quote: Large, overgrown lilacs, honeysuckles, dogwoods, spireas, barberry, flowering quince, ninebark, smokebush, and forsythias may be pruned in this manner. Spring-blooming shrubs like ninebark, smokebush, and forsythia will not bloom the following spring after renovation pruning.

Taxus.note: 8 plants. Yew; one of the few evergreens capable of resprouting from bare wood, though slowly.

general.note: Unlike most evergreens, yew can initiate new growth from bare stems and may eventually fill in a hard-pruned gap, though this can take considerable time.

source.title: Pruning Large, Overgrown Shrubs — Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
source.quote: Some species, such as yew and, to a lesser extent, boxwood and arborvitae, can initiate new growth from bare stems and may eventually fill in, but this process can take considerable time.

Buxus.note: 7 plants. Boxwood; marginally hardy in the Upper Midwest and prone to winter dieback that needs corrective pruning.

earlySpring.note: Assess winter injury in early spring; where dieback has occurred, prune back to live wood and give the plant a chance to recover.

source.title: Managing Winter Injury to Boxwood — Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
source.quote: When this happens, prune back to the live wood and give them a chance to recover.

Aronia.note: Suckering colonial shrub; remove root suckers to control spread unless a naturalized thicket is wanted.

general.note: Remove root suckers to prevent colonial spread unless naturalized spread is desired.

source.title: Aronia melanocarpa - Plant Finder
source.quote: Remove root suckers to prevent colonial spread unless desired.

Athyrium.note: Divide clumps periodically in spring to keep crowns at soil level.

earlySpring.note: Divide clumps in spring every few years to reposition crowns at the soil level.

source.title: Athyrium filix-femina - Plant Finder
source.quote: Divide clumps in spring every few years to reposition crowns at the soil level.

Eupatorium.note: Cut to the ground in late winter ahead of new spring growth.

lateFall.note: Cut plants to the ground in late winter.

source.title: Eutrochium maculatum - Plant Finder
source.quote: Cut plants to the ground in late winter.

Hamamelis.note: Suckering shrub needing little pruning; remove suckers promptly and prune only lightly if needed.

general.note: Promptly remove suckers to prevent colonial spread.

source.title: Hamamelis virginiana - Plant Finder
source.quote: Promptly remove suckers to prevent colonial spread.

earlySpring.note: Little pruning is required. Prune in early spring if necessary.

source.title: Hamamelis virginiana - Plant Finder
source.quote: Little pruning is required. Prune in early spring if necessary.

Heliopsis.note: Deadhead to extend bloom; cut back in late May to reduce final height.

midSummer.note: Remove spent flowers to extend bloom season.

source.title: Heliopsis helianthoides - Plant Finder
source.quote: Remove spent flowers to extend bloom season.

lateSpring.note: Plant stems may be cut back by 1/3 to 1/2 in late May to reduce overall plant height.

source.title: Heliopsis helianthoides - Plant Finder
source.quote: Plant stems may be cut back by 1/3 to 1/2 in late May to reduce overall plant height.

Buddleia.note: Often dies back in this region; cut close to the ground in late winter, deadhead through summer, and remove spent flowers before seed forms to limit self-seeding.

lateFall.note: Plants often grow more vigorously, produce superior flowers and maintain better shape if cut close to the ground in late winter each year.

source.title: Buddleja davidii - Plant Finder
source.quote: Even if plants do not die to the ground in winter, they often grow more vigorously, produce superior flowers and maintain better shape if cut close to the ground in late winter each year.

midSummer.note: Prompt removal of spent flower spikes during the growing season will usually encourage continued bloom until frost.

source.title: Buddleja davidii - Plant Finder
source.quote: Prompt removal of spent flower spikes during the growing season will usually encourage continued bloom until frost.

midSummer.note: Where self-seeding is a potential problem, remove spent flower clusters prior to formation/disbursement of seed.

source.title: Buddleja davidii - Plant Finder
source.quote: Where self-seeding is a potential problem, remove spent flower clusters prior to formation/disbursement of seed.

Lavandula.note: Deadhead to prolong bloom; shape in spring and hard-prune every few years to keep plants from getting woody.

midSummer.note: Remove faded flowers to promote continued bloom.

source.title: Lavandula angustifolia - Plant Finder
source.quote: Remove faded flowers to promote continued bloom.

earlySpring.note: Prune to shape in spring after new leaves appear. Prune back to 8 inches in spring every 3 years to control plant size and to promote robust, new growth.

source.title: Lavandula angustifolia - Plant Finder
source.quote: Prune to shape in spring after new leaves appear. Prune back to 8” in spring every 3 years to control plant size and to promote robust, new growth.

Stachys.note: Lamb’s-ear type, grown for its silvery foliage mat; pick off damaged leaves in humid spells and remove flowering stems to keep the ground-cover effect.

midSummer.note: If mid-summer foliage decline occurs, pick off damaged leaves as needed.

source.title: Stachys byzantina - Plant Finder
source.quote: If mid-summer foliage decline occurs, pick off damaged leaves as needed.

midSummer.note: Many gardeners prefer to remove the flowering stems as they appear to enhance the ground cover effect.

source.title: Stachys byzantina - Plant Finder
source.quote: Many gardeners prefer to remove the flowering stems as they appear to enhance the ground cover effect.

Stachys.note: Betony type, grown for its flower spikes; cut back spent flowering stalks to encourage reblooming.

midSummer.note: Cut back the flowering stalks to encourage reblooming.

source.title: Stachys officinalis 'Hummelo' - Plant Finder
source.quote: Cut back the flowering stalks to encourage reblooming.

Tiarella.note: Removing spent flower spikes after bloom improves the appearance of the foliage mound.

lateSpring.note: Removal of flower spikes after bloom will improve the appearance of the foliage mound.

source.title: Tiarella cordifolia - Plant Finder
source.quote: Removal of flower spikes after bloom will improve the appearance of the foliage mound.

Clethra.note: Suckering shrub; remove suckers promptly unless a naturalized colony is wanted, and prune in late winter if needed.

general.note: Promptly remove root suckers unless naturalized look is desired.

source.title: Clethra alnifolia - Plant Finder
source.quote: Promptly remove root suckers unless naturalized look is desired.

lateFall.note: Prune if needed in late winter.

source.title: Clethra alnifolia - Plant Finder
source.quote: Prune if needed in late winter.

Delphinium.note: Cut back spent flower spikes promptly after bloom to encourage a later rebloom.

midSummer.note: After bloom, promptly cut back spent flower spikes to the basal foliage to encourage an additional late summer and/or fall bloom.

source.title: Delphinium elatum - Plant Finder
source.quote: After bloom, promptly cut back spent flower spikes to the basal foliage to encourage an additional late summer and/or fall bloom.

Rhus.note: Thicket-forming shrub that spreads aggressively by root suckers; remove suckers to keep it in bounds.

general.note: Species plants may spread aggressively by root suckers.

source.title: Rhus typhina - Plant Finder
source.quote: Species plants may spread aggressively by root suckers.

Vernonia.note: Cut back stems in late spring to reduce mature height; remove flower heads before seed sets to prevent unwanted self-seeding.

lateSpring.note: Overall plant height may be reduced by cutting back stems in late spring.

source.title: Vernonia fasciculata - Plant Finder
